name: Mullvad
facts: 5 euros a month, VAT included.
Pay with cash, Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash, Monero, bank wire, card, PayPal and more.
No email: your account is a random number.
Says it has had external audits since 2018, the latest in 2024.

name: IVPN
facts: Sign-up needs no email.
Pay with cash, Monero or Bitcoin.
Says it has had eight audits since 2019.
Says of itself: "We don't promise anonymity."
IVPN Limited is registered in Gibraltar.

name: Obscura VPN
facts: 8 dollars a month.
Pay with card, Bitcoin over Lightning or Monero.
Two-party relay: Obscura passes your connection to a Mullvad exit server and cannot read it.
App code is public. Its site mentions no audit.

name: Proton VPN
facts: Pay with card, PayPal, Bitcoin, cash or bank transfer. Bitcoin needs a free account first.
Says its apps are open source and independently audited.
Says Swiss law lets it keep no connection logs.

name: NordVPN
facts: Pay with cryptocurrency (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin and a stablecoin), card or PayPal.
Says independent firms audited its no-logs claim five times, the latest in 2024.
Its Linux apps are open source. Its Trust Center does not say the same for other platforms.
Company based in Panama.

name: Xeovo
facts: No email needed.
Pay with cash, Monero, Bitcoin, Litecoin, card or PayPal.
4.99 euros a month, less on longer plans.
Says it has a strict no-log policy.
Company based in Finland.

name: LNVPN
facts: lnvpn.net now redirects to nadanada.me.
"No account, no email, no ID checks, no KYC."
Pay with Bitcoin, Lightning, Monero or Zcash, from one day to one year. About 3 dollars a month.
Says it never logs activity or connection data on its infrastructure.

name: TunnelBear
facts: Free plan with 2 GB of data. Unlimited plan from 3.33 dollars a month.
Its payment page shows Visa, Mastercard and American Express.
Its site does not say whether an email or an account is needed.

name: Meile dVPN
facts: Decentralised VPN on the Sentinel blockchain.
Pay in cryptocurrency only. Fiat money is not accepted.
Desktop apps for Windows, macOS, Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and Arch.
Its page links to GitHub but states no license.

name: Tor Browser
facts: Free browser for desktop and Android.
The Tor Project also offers Tor VPN, in beta on Android.

name: Orbot
facts: Sends traffic from any app on Android and iOS through Tor.
Android lets you pick which apps use Tor.
Supports bridges and onion services.

name: Onion Browser
facts: Browser for iOS that connects through Tor. Free.
Made by Mike Tigas, Benjamin Erhart and the Guardian Project.

name: Snowflake
facts: Connects you to Tor where Tor is blocked.
Routes through volunteer proxies in uncensored countries and looks like a video or voice call.

name: I2P
facts: Decentralised network for private websites, messaging and file sharing.
Software is open source.

name: Freenet
facts: Peer-to-peer network for censorship-resistant publishing and communication, running since 1999.
The project calls itself Hyphanet, formerly Freenet.
Windows, Linux, macOS and other Unix systems.

name: Quad9
facts: Free. No sign-up, no account.
Says no data containing your IP address is ever logged in any Quad9 system.
Run by a not-for-profit foundation based in Zurich.
Blocks known malicious domains.

name: Control D
facts: Supports DNS over HTTPS/3, TLS and QUIC.
Keeps query logs for 30 days on every plan.
Free trial without a card, then priced per device.
Its site does not state the company's jurisdiction.

name: NextDNS
facts: Blocks threats, ads and trackers. Supports DNS over HTTPS and TLS.
You set log retention from one hour to two years, or turn logs off.
You pick where logs are stored: United States, European Union, United Kingdom or Switzerland.
You can start without signing up, but need an account to save settings.

name: RethinkDNS
facts: DNS resolver and firewall app for Android.
The app is free. The cloud DNS has a free and a paid tier.
Supports DNS over HTTPS and TLS and more than 190 blocklists.

name: DNSCrypt-Proxy
facts: Flexible DNS proxy for DNSCrypt v2, DNS over HTTPS, Anonymized DNSCrypt and Oblivious DoH.
Pre-built binaries for Android, BSD, Linux, macOS and Windows.
ISC license.

name: Unbound
facts: Validating, recursive, caching DNS resolver.

name: Pi-hole
facts: Network-wide ad blocking.

name: ipleak.net
facts: Tests your IP addresses, DNS resolvers, WebRTC and torrent exposure.
Runs on AirVPN, a VPN company.

name: dnsleaktest.com
facts: DNS leak test that also shows your IP address and approximate location.
Its footer names IVPN Limited.

name: Cover Your Tracks
facts: Shows how trackers see your browser and which of its traits identify you.
Run by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

name: AmIUnique
facts: Checks your browser fingerprint.
Research project listing a French university contact (Lille).

name: Mullvad Check
facts: Tests for DNS and WebRTC leaks. Needs JavaScript.
Run by Mullvad, a VPN company.

name: OpenWrt
facts: Linux operating system for routers and other embedded devices, extended with packages.
GPL-2.0 license.

name: OPNsense
facts: Open source firewall and routing platform.
BSD 2-clause license.

name: Sparrow
facts: Bitcoin wallet for desktop with Tor built in.
Works with the common hardware wallets, over USB or air-gapped.
Full control of coins and fees. Connects to Bitcoin Core or private Electrum servers.
Apache 2 license.

name: Electrum
facts: Bitcoin wallet for Linux, Windows, macOS and Android.
Says your private keys are encrypted and never leave your computer.
Supports cold storage, multisig and recovery from a seed phrase.
MIT license.

name: Wasabi
facts: Bitcoin wallet for desktop with Tor and CoinJoin.
Coinjoin coordinators are third parties that you must find yourself.
Desktop only: Windows, macOS and Linux. No mobile app.
MIT license.

name: Edge
facts: Self-custody wallet for iOS, Android and the web.
Sign up with a username and password. Its page does not mention email.
Buying inside the app goes through partners (Banxa, MoonPay, Paybis). Its page does not mention KYC.

name: Cake Wallet
facts: Non-custodial wallet for Bitcoin, Monero, Litecoin, Ethereum, Zcash and more.
iOS, Android and Linux.
Buying and swapping happen through third parties at their rates and terms.
MIT license.

name: Trezor
facts: Says its code and design are 100% open source. Sold since 2013.
Says private keys are generated in the device and held only by you.
Its page cites no independent audit.

name: BitBox
facts: Swiss hardware wallet. The Bitcoin-only edition runs firmware that supports only Bitcoin.
Says the firmware is open source with reproducible builds and a bug bounty.
Our checker could not open this site, so these points come from the page as indexed by a search engine.

name: Satochip
facts: Hardware wallet in the form of an NFC smartcard with an EAL6+ certified secure element.
Says its software is open source.
Its page lists no price.

name: KeepKey
facts: Hardware wallet sold by KEEPKEY LLC, founded in 2014.
Says its firmware is open source and the hardware fully auditable.

name: Ledger
facts: Non-custodial hardware wallets with a secure element chip.
Its site calls the Ledger operating system proprietary and makes no open source claim.

name: imKey
facts: Hardware wallet with an Infineon secure element certified CC EAL6+.
Its site does not name a manufacturer and does not mention open source.

name: Monero (official wallet)
facts: The official Monero client, downloaded from getmonero.org.
The site links to the project's source code on GitHub.

name: Feather Wallet
facts: Free, open source Monero wallet for Linux, Tails, Windows and macOS.
Built to be easy for beginners, configurable for stricter threat models.
BSD-3 license.

name: Cake Wallet
facts: Non-custodial wallet that also holds Monero. iOS, Android and Linux.
MIT license.

name: Monerujo
facts: Free, open source Monero wallet for Android.
Offers KYC-free swaps through Exolix.
Its footer reads "© 2024".

name: Aeonujo
facts: Android wallet for Aeon, published by the Monerujo organisation on GitHub.
Described as "monerujoAE: An Android AEON Wallet". Apache 2 license.
No dedicated website. Last code change: May 2021.

name: Monero
facts: Describes itself as a private, decentralised cryptocurrency that keeps finances confidential.
Source code on GitHub.

name: Zcash
facts: Describes itself as encrypted electronic cash and the first cryptocurrency with zero-knowledge encryption.
Wallets named on its site: Zodl (Zashi) and Edge.
The original zcash/zcash repository on GitHub is archived.

name: Firo
facts: Describes itself as a digital currency focused on privacy, built on Lelantus Spark.
Says balances, history and recipients are hidden by default.
MIT license.

name: MySudo
facts: App that gives each identity its own phone number, email address and virtual cards.
Says it never requires your personal email or phone number to get started.
Phone numbers in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada (limited). UK numbers require legal identity information.

name: Coincards
facts: Buy gift cards, top-ups and prepaid vouchers with Bitcoin. No bank required.
Over 20 countries.
Its page does not mention accounts or KYC.

name: Privacy.com
facts: Virtual cards that hide your real payment details from merchants.
United States residents only. Requires a KYC check and a US bank account.

name: Tails
facts: Starts from a USB stick instead of Windows, macOS or Linux.
Uses the Tor network for everything you do online.
Says it leaves no trace on the computer when you shut it down.
Free software that independent researchers can verify.

name: Whonix
facts: Routes all internet traffic through Tor with a dual-VM design.
Runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, Qubes, KVM, USB, ISO and Raspberry Pi.
Says all its source code uses OSI approved licenses.

name: Qubes OS
facts: Free and open source system built on compartmentalization.
Brings the security of the Xen hypervisor to personal computers.
Its home page links to a separate page for hardware requirements.

name: Kicksecure
facts: Secure by default system based on Debian.
Runs on a physical computer, from a USB stick or in a virtual machine.
Says all its source code uses OSI approved licenses.

name: secureblue
facts: Security-focused desktop and server Linux system built on Fedora Atomic Desktop images.
Developed as an open source project. Apache 2 license.

name: Fedora Workstation
facts: GNOME desktop built on open source technology.
Says it is free, has no ads and that your data belongs to you.

name: openSUSE Tumbleweed
facts: Continuously updated: you install it once.
Its page links to the source code and to a license page.

name: Arch Linux
facts: Independently developed x86-64 GNU/Linux distribution with a rolling release.
Minimal base system: you add only the software you need.

name: NixOS
facts: Linux system configured declaratively with Nix.
Says a package that works on one machine works on another.
Nix is LGPL 2.1 and Nixpkgs is MIT.

name: Debian
facts: Calls itself a complete Free Operating System, built by a community of people.

name: OpenBSD
facts: Free, multi-platform Unix-like operating system based on 4.4BSD.
Says: "Only two remote holes in the default install, in a heck of a long time!"
Developed by volunteers and funded by donations.

name: FreeBSD
facts: Operating system known for network performance and stability.
BSD-style license that allows redistribution and modification.

name: GrapheneOS
facts: Privacy and security focused mobile system that runs Android apps.
Supports Pixel devices only, from the Pixel 6 series to the Pixel 10a.
Says it will never include Google Play services or microG.
Non-profit open source project.

name: CalyxOS
facts: Android system focused on privacy and security.
Supports Pixel 6 to 10a, Fairphone 5 and 6, some Motorola phones and the SHIFTphone 8.
Offers microG as an option. Its latest news item, dated 1 October 2026, is the Android 17 rollout.
Links to its source code on GitLab.

name: /e/OS
facts: Open source mobile system with selected apps.
Says its Android core has no Google apps or Google services accessing your data.
Installs on supported devices through a web installer.

name: LineageOS
facts: Android distribution with a wide list of supported phones, from Pixel and Samsung to Fairphone.
Its device wiki says a device that is not listed is not supported.
Our checker could not open the main site, so these points come from its device wiki.

name: Posteo
facts: 1 euro a month.
Pay anonymously: its page says no payment data connects to an account.
Says it collects no personal information at sign-up.
Based in Berlin, with servers in German data centres.
Supports PGP and S/MIME encryption.

name: Proton Mail
facts: Free plan with 1 GB and one address.
End-to-end and zero-access encryption.
Open source apps for web, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iPhone.
Headquartered in Switzerland.
Its page does not say whether sign-up needs a phone number.

name: Tuta
facts: Free plan. Paid plans add custom domains.
End-to-end encryption with post-quantum algorithms.
Says all its clients are open source. Made in Germany.
Its page does not say what sign-up requires.

name: Mailbox.org
facts: From 1 euro a month. 30-day free trial, no free plan.
Data stored in German data centres.
Its page does not state sign-up requirements or accepted payment methods.

name: Disroot
facts: Email, cloud, chat, pads and more from a platform funded by donations.
Says: no tracking, no ads, no profiling, no data mining.
Its page does not state sign-up rules or jurisdiction.

name: addy.io
facts: Creates aliases that forward to your real inbox. You can turn off any alias that gets spammy.
Free plan: unlimited standard aliases, 10 shared-domain aliases, 1 recipient and 10 MB of bandwidth a month.
Paid plans from 1 dollar a month, billed yearly.
Open source, with a self-hosting option.

name: SimpleLogin
facts: Email aliases that forward to your inbox and let you reply from the alias.
Says it is 100% open source, with the code on GitHub.
Product of Proton AG, a Swiss company.

name: Wasabi
facts: Desktop Bitcoin wallet with Tor, coin control and CoinJoin through the WabiSabi protocol.
Says CoinJoin coordination is run by third parties that you must find yourself.
Windows, macOS and Linux. No mobile app.
MIT license.

name: JoinMarket
facts: Software that creates CoinJoin transactions through a market: makers wait to take part, takers pay them a fee.
The repository has been archived since April 2026 and its README says it is not recommended for use.
GPL-3.0 license.
